sections.sectionText: Great American cases is a lecture that covers great cases and trials in the United States, in chronological order and with context of how they shape the American legal tradition. A case will be assigned for each class, allowing students to gain skills in reading case law and primary legal documents. Cases will be briefed in the lecture, allowing students to learn more about black letter law in a variety of legal fields, focusing on constitutional law and criminal procedure. Students will be graded on the basis of a midterm and final that will be closed book, in person, multiple-choice scantron exam. The course will attempt to historicize important trends in US jurisprudence, illustrating what former president Barak Obama meant when he asserted: "The law is also memory; the law also records a long-running conversation, a nation arguing with its conscience.” In addition to learning more about historic US and Illinois cases, students will learn two crucial skills that transfer to law school if they choose to pursue the study of law. Students will practice reading cases and be able to self-assess their evaluations of the texts over the semester. Students will also be required to memorize case names, holding, rationale and dissents in order to answer multiple choice exams, simulating the black letter law retention skill which is necessary in law school and for the bar exam for admission to the practice of law.

sections.sectionText: Law 798 Comparative Analysis of Legal Practice is an individual research and writing offering designed to lend flexibility to the law school program. It is intended for international students who have a strong research and writing interest in a topic not covered by the curriculum. This course is eligible to pair with an application for CPT status. Non-international students wishing to pursue similar topics may enroll in the Law 699 course. A student wishing to write a research paper for this course credit should identify a faculty member willing to supervise the project. The student and faculty supervisor will work out the details of the project, including the scope of the paper, the number of hours of credit, and any other requirements. After working out these details, the student should fill out a petition for Law 798 Comparative Analysis of Legal Practice credit (available on the College of Law intranet), and turn it in to the Dean of Students. The faculty supervisor must approve and sign the petition before it is submitted to the Dean of Students. The faculty has adopted these guidelines concerning Law 798 Comparative Analysis of Legal Practice: (1) Two hours of credit for this course, cumulatively, is the total allowable maximum. This cumulative two credit hour cap is inclusive of any Law 699 credits as well. (2) This course is not available to students on academic probation. (3) To earn one credit hour, the student usually must produce a research paper of at least 20 pages (excluding footnotes). To earn two credit hours, the student usually must produce a research paper of at least 40 pages (excluding footnotes). (4) Most students will require at least 60 hours of writing and research to complete a one-credit Independent Study project, and at least 120 hours to complete a two-credit project. But in no event will the student receive credit without devoting at least 45 hours per credit to the project. To ensure that this minimum 45-hour requirement is satisfied, the student must keep a record of time devoted to the project. (5) The supervisor must be a University of Illinois Law faculty member. Students may use Law 699 to satisfy the upper-level writing requirement. In that case, the project must also satisfy the guidelines of that writing requirement.
